limitations: No published slope limit exists for a crewed Mars rover or for suited walking on Mars. The limits used come from the Apollo rover (Moon, 1/6 g), the Artemis suit requirement (Moon) and NASA's robotic Mars rovers.
Slope does not show soil type. The same vehicle can be stopped by loose sand at low slopes, or can exceed 30° on solid rock.
Rocks smaller than about 1 m (obstacle limits are 0.3–0.5 m) can't be seen in these elevation models.
A single 18 m cell's slope is uncertain by several degrees (HiRISE vs CTX RMSE 3.6–8.0°).
HiRISE elevation models contain straight-line artifacts that can look like steep lines; they are not flagged.
Only craters ≥ 1 km are catalogued (Robbins & Hynek 2012).
West Candor has no rover ground truth. In Gale, no HiRISE model covers Curiosity's route.
A drawn route is never verified safe. Grey (unknown) areas have no elevation data.
The steepest spot in a 1 km square is a single value and is often an elevation-model artifact. The 95th-percentile slope given with each point describes the square better.
The elevation models overstate steep ground: the rovers recorded gentler tilt than the models show at the same places.
Slope is not computed next to data gaps (within about 15 m for HiRISE and 18 m for CTX), because nothing is filled in.
Overlapping elevation models disagree in absolute height by tens of metres. Heights come from one model at a time and are never merged.
Where elevation models overlap, the most detailed one with data is used: HiRISE (slope over 5 m) before CTX (slope over 18 m). The two baselines give different slope values for the same ground.
The roughness and relief floors are placeholders chosen during processing, not published limits.
Geology comes from a 1:20,000,000 global map and gives regional context only.
